The method is clear and everyone agrees on it: it is a syllabic charade and *quodque fit ex illis* is built in the order the verse prescribes, with *Didonis prima sequatur* doing real work.

The point on which the whole concatenation stands is the cut of *Penelopes primam*. The verse does not give us an abstract lemma Penelope, it gives us the form as it stands in the line, *Penelopes*. In the line that is *Pen-e-lo-pes*. The first spoken chunk you get off that genitive is *Pen-*, not an isolated *Pe-* that would require detaching the *n* that belongs to the onset of the name.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* then means: take that whole first chunk of Penelopes and let the first chunk of Didonis follow it. That is *Pen-* + *Di-* = *Pen-Di-* at the head of the charade, as 13 and 14 put it. If we keep the natural first syllable of the form as written, we do not then truncate it to *Pe-*.

Once *Pen-Di-* is established the verse order is fixed: *et primam Cadmi* = *Ca-* and *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*, the two pieces added in that order. We do not truncate *Didonis* to *Di-* with a detached *do*, we do not truncate *Remi* to *Re-* with a detached *mi*, so there is no licence to treat *Penelopes* differently.

In the order the poet sets out we therefore get

*Pen-* + *Di-* + *Ca-* + *Re-* = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*

i.e. *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.

That is the word the speaker says *mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. 

*Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* is the familiar school-book gloss and it is very attractive because of the *pedica / paedicare* pun that is rightly noted by 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18. It is the traditional reception of the epigram. But that reading depends on cutting *Penelopes primam* down to an artificial *Pe-* truncation in order to make the nice *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* sequence work. On a strictly literal first-syllable-as-written reading, with consistent treatment of the four names and with *sequatur* respected, the concatenation the riddle actually builds is *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*.

I would like the *Pe-* camp to show how *Pe-* is the natural *primam* of *Penelopes* as written *Pen-e-lo-pes* given the consistent treatment of *Cadmi* and *Remi* in the same verse. Until that metrical/phonological justification is given, the faithful literal charade is *pendicare*.

I think we have to settle the actual cut of *Penelopes primam* before we lock the lemma, because the whole concatenation depends on it.

The verse orders the pieces explicitly: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*. That is not “normalise to the nominative lemma and pick a convenient syllable”, it is take the form as it stands in the line and let the next piece follow it.

In the line the form is *Penelopes*, genitive, and the first spoken chunk you get off that word is *Pen-*, *Pen-e-lo-pes*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole first chunk, so the head of the charade is *Pen-Di-* on a literal reading. We do not truncate *Didonis* to *Di-* with a detached *do*, we do not read *Remi* as *Re-* with a detached *mi*, and we should not license a different cut for the first name.

Once *Pen-Di-* is kept, the verse order is fixed: *primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-* in the order named. That gives

*Pen-* + *Di-* + *Ca-* + *Re-* = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*, i.e. *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.

The *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* reading is very familiar, and the *pedica* fettering / *paedicare* vulgar pun is why the epigram is traditionally quoted that way. It only works if we artificially truncate the natural first syllable *Pen-* to *Pe-* in order to get the nice *Pe-Di-* sequence. That is the truncation already flagged by 2, 9, 13 and 14, and it is not licensed by *sequatur*.

If we keep the literal first syllable of each name as it appears in the line and respect the ordering the poet insists on, the charade the riddle builds is *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* and the penalty announced to the *fur deprensus in horto* who is told *dabis mihi : hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is that form. Can the *Pe-* camp show a clear metrical/phonological justification for reading *Penelopes primam* as *Pe-* rather than the natural *Pen-* in situ, given we are not making the same truncation for *Didonis*, *Cadmi* and *Remi*?

public_text.13:
I’m trying to keep the charade strictly literal, in the order the verse actually prescribes it, and that’s where the segmentation of Penelopes primam seems to decide everything.

The verse is explicit about order: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*. It is not “give me an abstract lemma and pick a convenient syllable”, it is take the first piece of the form as it stands in the line and put the first piece of the next name after it.

The form as it stands in the line is *Penelopes*. In the line that is the genitive *Pen-e-lo-pes*. The first spoken chunk you get off that genitive is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then does real work: Di- is to follow that whole first chunk, so we get *Pen-Di-* at the head of the charade, exactly as colleagues 13, 14, 2 and 9 have been stressing.

Once that is fixed the rest of the verse is treated consistently in the order it names them: *et primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*. No further truncation is applied to Cadmi or Remi, and we are not asked to detach *do* from *Didonis*.

That gives in the poet’s own order

*Pen-* + *Di-* + *Ca-* + *Re-* = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*

i.e. *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis* which the speaker says the *fur deprensus in horto* will *dabis mihi: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

The familiar *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* reading is the one the school tradition quotes, and the *pedica/pedicari* fettering and later vulgar pun are very real and famous. It only works, however, if we first truncate *Penelopes primam* down to *Pe-*, i.e. amputate the *n* that belongs to the onset of the name as written in the genitive, in order to get *Pe-Di-*.

I’m not seeing a principled reason for that selective truncation: why is *Penelopes* allowed to become *Pe-*, while *Cadmi* stays *Ca-* and not *Ca-d-*, *Remi* stays *Re-* and not *Re-mi-*, and *Didonis* stays *Di-* and not *Di-do-*? If we are going to insist on a literal first syllable as pronounced in the line, *Pen-* is the natural first syllable of *Penelopes*, not an isolated *Pe-* that is required to make *pedicare*.

Can someone show a clear metrical/phonological justification for *Pe-* as the *primam* of *Penelopes* as written *Penelopes*, given *Pen-e-lo-pes* in situ, and why that cut is licensed here but not the analogous cuts for the other three names? Keeping the natural first syllable of each name and respecting *sequatur* makes the charade consistent, and on that consistent literal reading the word the verse builds is *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The method is stable: a syllabic charade built in the verse order *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*, and *quodque fit ex illis* is the word the *fur deprensus in horto* is told he will *dabis mihi* and with which *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Core lexical content is settled: *pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks; *pedicare* = to put in a *pedica*, to fetter the feet, *pedicari* to be fettered/put in stocks. The same form is the classical/medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise/be buggered’, so the *in horto* context gives the famous dirty garden pun. The passive/deponent sense inflicted on the thief is *pedicari/pedicatus*.

The live split remains syllabification of *Penelopes primam* and consistency of the cut with *sequatur*.

Pe- camp – Colleagues 1,4,6,7,10-12,15-18 and now also 3,4 – reads Latin scansion *Pe-ne-lo-pe*, *Penelopes* = *Pe-ne-lo-pes*. First metrical syllable is *Pe-*. Then *Didonis prima sequatur* = *Di-* follows it, *primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*. *Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re-* = *pedicare*. This is the received school-room tradition and the attested lemma on which the epigram is famously quoted, with literal fettering and the customary obscene double sense. They argue *n* is onset of second syllable *-ne-*, so no truncation is needed, and *sequatur* is satisfied.

Pen- camp – Colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14 – insists the *primam* must be taken as written in the line, *Penelopes*. The first spoken chunk of the genitive is *Pen-*, *Pen-e-lo-pes*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk, giving *Pen-Di-* at the head. *et primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*. In verse order *Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re-* = *pendicare*. The Pe- reading is said to require an artificial truncation *Pen-* → *Pe-*, i.e. amputating the *n* that belongs to the onset, a cut not applied to *Didonis, Cadmi, Remi*. *sequatur* is taken as evidence for keeping the whole first chunk. Colleagues 1,7,18 now explicitly concede that on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.

Changes in round 3: Colleague 3 abandoned the earlier *deprecari* chain and now aligns with Pe- camp; Colleague 4 now states the received tradition is *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* while acknowledging the Pen- literal reading. No new lexical challenge to *pedicare/pedicari* sense.

Unresolved: whether Latin metrical first syllable of *Penelopes* is *Pe-* or phonetic first chunk *Pen-*. If strict first-chunk-as-written is kept consistently with the three other names, the verse builds *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*; if traditional Latin scansion *Pe-ne-* is kept, the verse builds the familiar *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedicari* with its fettering/stocks sense and customary obscene garden pun. My current belief remains that the intended, traditionally cited charade is *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare*, literally ‘to be fettered/put in foot-irons/stocks’ and conventionally received as the obscene ‘to be buggered’ garden punishment, while the Pen- vs Pe- syllabification objection is the principal remaining contention and would give *pendicare* on a strictly literal first-chunk reading.

reflection_text.15:
The charade is syllabic and ordered by the verse: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis...* The penalty is the word built from those four pieces and the phrase *mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Received school tradition, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7:
*Penelopes* in Latin scansion is Pe-ne-lo-pes, *Penelope* Pe-ne-lo-pe. The first metrical/syllabic piece of the genitive as it stands in the line is therefore Pe-, not an English eye-chunk Pen-. *Didonis prima sequatur* makes Di- follow Pe-, *primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-. In verse order Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.
*pedica* f. = foot-fetter, shackle, stocks. *pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks/irons; *pedicari* to be fettered. Formal school-book poena = fettering/shackling/being put in the stocks. The same form is the classical-medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise’, whence the traditional jocular quotation *in horto eris pedicatus*: literal fettering, conventionally rendered as pedication/sodomy.

Competing literal-first-chunk reading, colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9:
The verse orders the pieces and *sequatur* does real work: take the first piece of the form as it stands in the line and let the next piece follow it. The form as written is *Penelopes* = Pen-e-lo-pes. The first spoken chunk you get off that genitive is Pen-. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces Di- to follow that whole chunk, giving Pen-Di- at the head. *primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- in the order named, with no further truncation of Didonis, Cadmi, Remi. This gives Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.
The *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* reading requires an artificial selective truncation Pen- → Pe- only for the first name to obtain the nice pun. Consistency argument: we do not truncate Didonis to Di- vs Di-do- nor Remi to Re- vs Re-mi-, so why truncate Penelopes? On strict first-syllable-as-written with sequatur respected, the literal concatenation is pendicare.

Current round 3 shows the split consolidating. 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 explicitly acknowledge the Pen- objection, concede that on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you get Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare, and defend Pe- by Latin quantitative syllabification Pe-ne-lo-pes and the attested tradition on which the epigram is universally cited. 13,14,2,5,8,9 press the consistency/sequatur point and argue the faithful literal charade is pendicare.

Unresolved:
* Philological cut of *Penelopes primam* in situ: Pe- by Latin scansion vs Pen- as first spoken chunk of the genitive as written; whether the *n* can be licensed as onset of the second syllable.
* Whether *sequatur* licenses the Pe- truncation or demands the Pen- chunk kept intact.
* Whether the intended sense is the literal foot-fettering/stocks or the vulgar sexual pun; historically they are linked.
* Whether received tradition *pedicare/pedicari* should override the stricter literal concatenation *pendicare*.

My current synthesis remains with the conventionally cited lemma Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicari*: fettering/shackling, traditionally quoted as the obscene garden pun. The Pen- → pendicare objection is a real syllabification/consistency problem that challenges the canonical reading, and the Pen- camp now has explicit concessions on the phonetic reading.
reflection_text.1:
The method is stable: a syllabic charade built in the verse order *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*, and *quodque fit ex illis* is the word the *fur deprensus in horto* is told he will *dabis mihi* and with which *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Core lexical content is settled: *pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks; *pedicare* = to put in a *pedica*, to fetter the feet, *pedicari* to be fettered/put in stocks. The same form is the classical/medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise/be buggered’, so the *in horto* context gives the famous dirty garden pun. The passive/deponent sense inflicted on the thief is *pedicari/pedicatus*.

The live split remains syllabification of *Penelopes primam* and consistency of the cut with *sequatur*.

Pe- camp – Colleagues 1,4,6,7,10-12,15-18 and now also 3,4 – reads Latin scansion *Pe-ne-lo-pe*, *Penelopes* = *Pe-ne-lo-pes*. First metrical syllable is *Pe-*. Then *Didonis prima sequatur* = *Di-* follows it, *primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*. *Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re-* = *pedicare*. This is the received school-room tradition and the attested lemma on which the epigram is famously quoted, with literal fettering and the customary obscene double sense. They argue *n* is onset of second syllable *-ne-*, so no truncation is needed, and *sequatur* is satisfied.

Pen- camp – Colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14 – insists the *primam* must be taken as written in the line, *Penelopes*. The first spoken chunk of the genitive is *Pen-*, *Pen-e-lo-pes*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk, giving *Pen-Di-* at the head. *et primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*. In verse order *Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re-* = *pendicare*. The Pe- reading is said to require an artificial truncation *Pen-* → *Pe-*, i.e. amputating the *n* that belongs to the onset, a cut not applied to *Didonis, Cadmi, Remi*. *sequatur* is taken as evidence for keeping the whole first chunk. Colleagues 1,7,18 now explicitly concede that on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.

Changes in round 3: Colleague 3 abandoned the earlier *deprecari* chain and now aligns with Pe- camp; Colleague 4 now states the received tradition is *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* while acknowledging the Pen- literal reading. No new lexical challenge to *pedicare/pedicari* sense.

Unresolved: whether Latin metrical first syllable of *Penelopes* is *Pe-* or phonetic first chunk *Pen-*. If strict first-chunk-as-written is kept consistently with the three other names, the verse builds *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*; if traditional Latin scansion *Pe-ne-* is kept, the verse builds the familiar *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedicari* with its fettering/stocks sense and customary obscene garden pun. My current belief remains that the intended, traditionally cited charade is *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare*, literally ‘to be fettered/put in foot-irons/stocks’ and conventionally received as the obscene ‘to be buggered’ garden punishment, while the Pen- vs Pe- syllabification objection is the principal remaining contention and would give *pendicare* on a strictly literal first-chunk reading.

The verse is a syllabic charade built in the order the verse imposes: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis…*.

Two competing segmentations remain.

Majority school-tradition reading, held in round 3 by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7:
Latin scansion *Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe, Penelopes = Pe-ne-lo-pes*. The *n* is onset of the second syllable *-ne-*, so the first metrical syllable that can be taken off the form as it stands in the line is *Pe-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* makes *Di-* follow *Pe-*; *primam Cadmi = Ca-*; *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in the order named.
Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re = *pedicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.
*Pedica* f. = foot-fetter, shackle, stocks; *pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks; *pedicari* passive/deponent the form actually suffered by the fur. That is the formal school-book poena: the thief deprensus in horto is threatened with being made pedicatus, fettered/shackled/put in foot-irons.
Same form carries the classical-medieval vulgar development *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise/be buggered’, whence the traditional jocular quotation *in horto eris pedicatus*.

Minority strict first-syllable-as-written reading, pressed in round 3 by Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9:
The form as written in the line is *Penelopes*. The first spoken chunk off *Pen-e-lo-pes* is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk, giving *Pen-Di-* at the head. With consistent treatment of the other names – *Cadmi = Ca-*, *Remi = Re-* – the verse order gives
Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*, the word the speaker says the fur will *dabis mihi: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

The objection acknowledged by the majority: on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. Colleagues 1,7,18 explicitly note the Pen- objection is real, but defend the received *Pe-* cut and the attested lemma *pedicare/pedicari* on which the epigram is universally cited. Colleague 3 has abandoned the earlier deprecari stem and aligned with Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare.

Unresolved: whether *Pe-* is a principled Latin first syllable of *Penelopes* in situ or an artificial truncation *Pen- → Pe-* licensed only for the first name. The consistency argument is that *Cadmi* is not cut to *Ca-d-*, *Remi* not to *Re-mi-*, *Didonis* not to *Di-do-*, so *Penelopes* should not be truncated. The Latin scansion defence is that *Pe-ne-lo-pes* is the normal Latin syllabification and *sequatur* is thereby satisfied without selective truncation.

Current belief: the overwhelming traditional gloss and citation of the epigram is *pedicare/pedicari*, literal fettering in the pedica/stocks with the customary obscene garden pun. The Pen- vs Pe- segmentation objection remains a serious philological challenge; on a literal first-syllable-as-written, consistent treatment the charade builds *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.

* syllaba prima Remi = Re-

The verse does not give us an abstract lemma *Penelope*, it gives us the form as it stands in the line: *Penelopes*. *Primam* here is the first piece of that form in situ. In the line we have *Pen-e-lo-pes*. The first spoken chunk you get off that genitive is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole first chunk, so the head of the charade is *Pen-Di-*.

*Pen-* + *Di-* + *Ca-* + *Re-* = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*,

I agree with the syllabic-charade reading and with the point that *sequatur* is doing real work. The verse tells us to build *quodque fit ex illis* in the order it names the four names, and *Didonis prima sequatur* is an ordering instruction, not a free permutation.

That makes the cut of *Penelopes primam* decisive. The verse does not give us an abstract lemma *Penelope*, it gives us the form as it stands in the line: *Penelopes*. *Primam* here is the first piece of that form in situ. In the line we have *Pen-e-lo-pes*. The first spoken chunk you get off that genitive is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole first chunk, so the head of the charade is *Pen-Di-*.

Once *Pen-Di-* is kept, the rest of the verse is treated consistently in the order it names them: *et primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*. We keep *Didonis* as *Di-*, *Cadmi* as *Ca-*, *Remi* as *Re-*. There is no licence to truncate those names, so there is no licence to truncate *Penelopes* differently.

In the poet’s own order that gives

*Pen-* + *Di-* + *Ca-* + *Re-* = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*,

i.e. *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*, the word the speaker says the *fur deprensus in horto* will *dabis mihi: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

The familiar *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* reading is the received school-room gloss and the *pedica / paedicare* fettering / vulgar pun is why the epigram is traditionally quoted that way. It only works if we amputate the *n* of the first name, *Pen- → Pe-*, in order to get the nice *Pe-Di-* sequence. Colleagues 1,7,18 have already conceded that on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.

I’m not seeing a principled reason for that selective truncation: why is *Penelopes* allowed to become *Pe-*, while *Cadmi* stays *Ca-* and not *Ca-d-*, *Remi* stays *Re-* and not *Re-mi-*, and *Didonis* stays *Di-* and not *Di-do-*? If we insist on a literal first syllable as pronounced in the line, *Pen-* is the natural first syllable of *Penelopes*, not an isolated *Pe-* required to make *pedicare*.

Keeping the natural first syllable of each name as it appears in the line and respecting *sequatur* makes the charade consistent, and on that consistent literal reading the word the verse actually builds out of *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is *pendicare*.

I think the discussion has now reached the point where the real hinge is on the table and it is worth staying with it clearly.

The method is no longer in dispute. It is a syllabic charade, *quodque fit ex illis* is to be built in the order the verse names the names, and *Didonis prima sequatur* is doing real work: the first piece of Didonis is to follow the first piece of Penelopes. We all agree on that.

What remains is what piece *Penelopes primam* actually is in the line as written. The form in the line is *Penelopes*, genitive, *Pen-e-lo-pes*. The first spoken chunk you get off that form in situ is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole first chunk, so the head of the charade is *Pen-Di-* on a literal first-chunk reading.

That is the reading colleagues 2,5,8,9,14 and I have been pressing, and I am grateful that colleagues 1,12 and 4 now explicitly concede the philological point: on a strictly phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. Colleague 12 puts it plainly: “on a strictly phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you do get Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare”. Colleague 1 and 18 record the same concession.

Once *Pen-Di-* is kept the rest follows in the poet’s own order without special pleading. *et primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*, taken in that order. We are not truncating *Didonis* to *Di-* with a detached *do-*, we are not reading *Remi* as *Re-* with a different cut, we are not cutting *Cadmi* to *Ca-d-*. The consistent treatment of the three unproblematic names makes the selective truncation of *Penelopes* only to *Pe-* stand out.

The *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* / *pedicari* reading is familiar, historically important, and it gives the famous *pedica* fettering / later vulgar garden pun on which the epigram is traditionally quoted. It only works if we first amputate the *n* that belongs to the onset of the name as written in the genitive, *Penelopes primam* → *Pe-*, in order to get the nice *Pe-Di-* sequence. That is an un-Latin cut licensed for the first name only.

Can the Pe- camp show a clear metrical/phonological justification for reading *Penelopes primam* as *Pe-* rather than the natural *Pen-* in situ, given we are not making the same truncation for *Didonis*, *Cadmi* and *Remi*? If *primam* means first syllable as it actually appears in the line, and *sequatur* means let the next piece follow it whole, then

*Pen-* + *Di-* + *Ca-* + *Re-* = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*

i.e. *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*, the word the speaker says the *fur deprensus in horto* will *dabis mihi: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

The traditional *pedicare/pedicari* lemma is the received school-room gloss and it is real, but it requires that selective Pe- truncation. On literal first-syllable fidelity to the forms as they appear in the verse, and on the *sequatur* ordering the poet insists on, the concatenation the verse actually builds is *pendicare*.

Two segmentations remain in play and have now crystallised.

Pe- camp – Colleagues 1,4,6,7,10-12,15-18 and now Colleague 3 – reads Latin scansion *Pe-ne-lo-pe*, *Penelopes = Pe-ne-lo-pes*. That is the received school-room tradition and attested lemma on which the epigram is famously quoted, with literal fettering/stocks sense and customary obscene double sense.

Pen- camp – Colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14 – insists *primam* must be taken of the form as written in the line, *Penelopes = Pen-e-lo-pes*. First spoken chunk in situ is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk, giving *Pen-Di-* at head. *et primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-*. 4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The riddle is a syllabic charade built from the four mythological names in verse order: Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis is the word the fur deprensus in horto is told he will dabis, hac poena culpa luenda tua est.

Method consensus persists: take first syllable piece of each name in the verse order, with Didonis prima sequatur forcing the Dido piece to follow the Penelope piece, and primam Cadmi followed by syllaba prima Remi in the order named.

Dominant tradition = Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare.
* pedica f. = foot-fetter, shackle, stocks; pedicare = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks; pedicari passive/deponent suffered.
Formal school gloss: thief caught in garden threatened with being made pedicatus, to be fettered/shackled/put in foot-irons.
Received jocular gloss: same form is classical/medieval vulgar paedicare/pedicare ‘to sodomise / to be buggered’; epigram traditionally quoted as dirty garden-penalty joke “you will be pedicated / buggered”.

This reading is defended by colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,4,6,7,3. Justification: Latin scansion Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe, so primam of Penelopes in the line is Pe-, not English-style Pen-. Pe- is then followed by Di-, then Ca-, then Re-.

Persistent minority segmentation dispute:
Colleagues 2,9,13,14,5,8 argue literal first spoken chunk of Penelopes as it stands in the line is Pen-, Pen-e-lo-pes. Sequatur then forces Pen- + Di- = Pen-Di-. With primam Cadmi = Ca- and syllaba prima Remi = Re- in order named, this gives Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare, quodque fit ex illis. They claim Pe- requires artificial truncation of natural first syllable Pen- to Pe-, inconsistent with how Didonis, Cadmi, Remi are treated.

Several majority colleagues now explicitly acknowledge the Pen- objection as real philologically. Colleague 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 note the Pe- cut is received school-room tradition that yields familiar attested lemma pedicare/pedicari on which epigram is famous, while conceding strict phonetic first-syllable reading would be Pen-Di-Ca-Re. Colleague 12: “The Pen- objection is real, and on a strictly phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you do get pendicare.” Colleague 1,18 record same concession.

Colleague 13,14 sharpen hinge: primam asked for of form as it stands in verse, Penelopes = Pen-e-lo-pes, first spoken chunk Pen-. Consistency requires same treatment for all four names; no licence to truncate Penelopes only.

Colleague 2,5,8,9 press consistency argument and note concessions, demanding clear metrical/phonological justification for reading Penelopes primam as Pe- rather than natural Pen- in situ, given no analogous truncation for Didonis, Cadmi, Remi.

Unresolved:
* Prosodic segmentation of Penelopes primam: natural Latin first metrical syllable Pe- vs literal first phonetic chunk Pen- as written; sequatur ordering.
* Which meaning is primary: literal fettering/pedicari vs well-known obscene double sense; group largely accepts both coexist, with literal fettering as formal gloss and obscene as traditional jocular reception, primacy remains open.
* Whether pendicare is strictly literal charade product and pedicare is later popularisation.

Remaining marginal proposals earlier: Colleague 3 deprecari chain, Colleague 5 pedicarem variant. In current round Colleague 3 now aligns with pedicare mainstream; Colleague 5 aligns with pendicare consistency argument.

Current best synthesis remains essentially Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare with fettering/shackling penalty, conventionally rendered as obscene pedication joke, while Pen- → pendicare segmentation objection remains consistently pressed by minority and is now explicitly recognized by majority as real philological issue.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The method is now stable across the group: a syllabic charade built in the verse order *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*, *quodque fit ex illis* = the word the *fur deprensus in horto* is told he will *dabis mihi* and with which *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. *Sequatur* is accepted as a real ordering instruction for the first two pieces.

Dispute is now only the cut of *Penelopes primam* and consistency.

Pe- camp – 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,4,6,7:
Latin quantitative scansion: *Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe*, genitive in line *Penelopes = Pe-ne-lo-pes*. *n* is onset of *-ne-*. First metrical syllable taken off the form as it stands is *Pe-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then puts *Di-* after it → *Pe-Di-*.
*primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in verse order.
Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = *pedicare, quodque fit ex illis*.
*pedica* f. = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter the feet, to put in stocks/foot-irons; *pedicari* to be fettered. That is the formal school-book poena, and the same lemma underlies the classical/medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise’, whence the traditional jocular reception *in horto eris pedicatus*.
This camp now explicitly concedes the Pen- objection: on a strict English phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you get *Pen-* and *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. The defence is that Latin scansion gives *Pe-*, not an English eye-chunk, and that the same principle gives *Ca-* for *Cadmi*, *Re-* for *Remi*, *Di-* for *Didonis*.

Pen- / consistency camp – 2,5,8,9,13,14:
Take the first spoken chunk of the form as it actually stands in the line. *Penelopes* in situ is *Pen-e-lo-pes*; first chunk is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk → *Pen-Di-* head.
Then *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in poet’s order.
Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.
Argument is consistency: why truncate *Penelopes* to *Pe-* while keeping *Didonis = Di-*, *Cadmi = Ca-*, *Remi = Re-* un-truncated? If *primam* means first piece of the form as written and *sequatur* means keep it whole, selective *Pen- → Pe-* is unlicensed. *pendicare* is the literal concatenation; no established lexical poena has been supplied for it, which is the main weakness of this camp.

Colleague 3 remains outlier with *deprecari* chain.

Unresolved hinge: whether *Penelopes primam* is legitimately *Pe-* by Latin scansion *Pe-ne-lo-pes* or must be taken as *Pen-* as written, and whether *sequatur* licenses a selective truncation only for the first name. The Pe- camp has the attested manuscript/school tradition *pedicare/pedicari* with fetter/obscene double sense; the Pen- camp has consistent first-syllable-as-written treatment and the explicit concessions that a phonetic first-chunk reading gives *pendicare*. No principled metrical/phonological justification for the selective *Pe-* cut versus consistent *Ca- / Re- / Di-* treatment has yet been shown to the satisfaction of the Pen- camp.

Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- camp
Colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14. Strictly phonetic first chunk of the form as written: *Penelopes* in situ is *Pen-e-lo-pes*, first spoken chunk *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* gives *Pen-Di-*. With *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in verse order: *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.

Evidence and concessions noted in round 4
* Pe- camp now explicitly states Latin quantitative syllabification *Pe-ne-lo-pes* with n onset of second syllable *-ne-*, hence first metrical syllable Pe-, and *sequatur* satisfied without special pleading. 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 repeat this and note the *Pen-* objection is the English first-phonetic-chunk reading.
* Multiple Pe- colleagues now concede the philological point: 1,12,18,1,7 etc acknowledge that on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. Colleague 12: “The Pen- objection is real, and on a strictly phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you do get pendicare.”
* 13 and 14 sharpen the hinge: *Penelopes primam* is asked for of the form in situ, not abstract lemma; first spoken chunk is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* forces *Pen-Di-*. Consistency requires same treatment for *Cadmi*/*Remi*/*Didonis*. They ask for explicit metrical/phonological justification for *Pen- → Pe-* selective cut.
* 2,5,8,9 press the same consistency demand and note the concessions. 2: selective truncation *Penelopes → Pe-* is un-Latin cut licensed for first name only.

Current status
Stable, historically attested solution taught and quoted is *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedicari*, punishment = to be fettered/shackled/put in the stocks, conventionally glossed as obscene pedicatio ‘to be sodomised/buggered’. The *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare* objection remains the main formal challenge, hinging on whether *Penelopes primam* is allowed to be scanned as Latin Pe- or must be taken as the English-looking phonetic chunk Pen-. Colleague 3 moved from deprecari in round 0 to Pe- in round 3 and remains Pe- in round 4. I remain with the Pe- reading as the intended charade and the historically cited lemma, while keeping the Pen- dissent, the explicit concessions about the strict first-chunk reading, and the unresolved question of a principled metrical/phonological justification for the selective Pe- cut versus consistent first-syllable-as-written treatment.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The charade is ordered *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis...* and the verse says the *fur deprensus in horto* will *dabis mihi* that word, *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Core dispute is segmentation of the first name.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,4,6,7: Latin quantitative scansion is decisive.
*Penelope* = Pe-ne-lo-pe, *Penelopes* in the line = Pe-ne-lo-pes. The n is onset of -ne-, so first metrical syllable is Pe-. *Didonis prima sequatur* orders Di- after Pe-, then *primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- in poet’s order. Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re = *pedicare*. 
*Pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks. *Pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter feet/put in stocks; deponent *pedicari* = to be so fettered. Classical-medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* = to sodomise. Hence the classic garden pun: literal fettering, jocularly buggered/pedicatio. This is the school-book gloss and manuscript tradition.

Pen-Di-Ca-Re camp, colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14: literal first-phonetic chunk of the form as written.
The form in the line is *Penelopes*, genitive *Pen-e-lo-pes*. First spoken chunk in situ is Pen-. *sequatur* does real work, so Pen- + Di- = Pen-Di- head. Then *et primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- treated consistently with no truncation of Didonis, Cadmi, Remi. Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = *pendicare*, unattested, the word *quodque fit ex illis* on a strict first-syllable-as-written reading.

Current round shift: Pe- defenders 1,10,11,12,4,7,18 now explicitly concede the philological point: on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare. They maintain Latin scansion licenses Pe- and the received tradition is built on the attested lemma *pedicare/pedicari*.

Unresolved:
1. Segmentation Pe- vs Pen- for *Penelopes primam*. Pe- camp cites Latin syllabification Pe-ne-lo-pes and consistent metrical treatment; Pen- camp cites consistent first-chunk-as-written treatment and the artificiality of amputating n only for the first name.
2. Semantic nuance: literal fettering vs vulgar sodomitical double entendre. Consensus is both co-exist for *pedicare*.

I am still leaning to the dominant consensus *pedicare/pedicari* as the intended word-play with literal fettering in the pedica/stocks and the customary vulgar double sense, because of attestation and the whole manuscript/school-room tradition. The Pen- vs Pe- philological objection is now explicitly conceded by multiple Pe- defenders and the demand for a principled, non-selective justification for reading *Penelopes primam* as Pe- rather than the natural Pen- in situ remains unmet. A consistent literal first-syllable-as-written reading with *sequatur* respected gives *pendicare*, unattested and sense-less, which is why the tradition settles on the Latin-scansion cut Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The charade is ordered by the verse *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis...* and the penalty is the word built from those four pieces, *mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Pe- camp 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18:

*Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re = pedicare, quodque fit ex illis*.
*pedica* f. = foot-fetter, shackle, stocks. *pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, put in stocks/foot-irons; *pedicari* to be so fettered. Formal school-book poena = fettering/shackling/being put in stocks.
That same form underlies classical-medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise’, whence traditional jocular citation *in horto eris pedicatus*: literal fettering, conventionally rendered as pedication/sodomy.

*Pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks. *Pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks/foot-irons; *pedicari* passive. That is the formal school-book poena: the thief is threatened with being made *pedicatus*, fettered/shackled/put in foot-irons/stocks, *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

reflection_text.6:
The verse is a syllabic charade ordered by the verse itself: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis…* and the word made is the *poena* the speaker says the *fur deprensus in horto* will *dabis mihi: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Two segmentations remain in play and have now crystallised.

Majority school-tradition reading, held in round 4 by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7:
Latin quantitative scansion *Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe*, *Penelopes = Pe-ne-lo-pes*. The *n* is onset of *-ne-*, so the first metrical syllable that can be taken off the form as it stands is *Pe-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* puts *Di-* after it. *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in poet’s order.
Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re = *pedicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.
*Pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks; *pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks; *pedicari* the passive/deponent form actually suffered. That is the formal school-book poena: the thief is threatened with being made *pedicatus*, fettered/shackled/put in foot-irons/stocks.
Same form carries the classical-medieval vulgar development *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise/be buggered’, whence the traditional jocular citation *in horto eris pedicatus*.

Minority strict first-syllable-as-written reading, pressed in round 4 by Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9:
The form in the line is *Penelopes*. The first spoken chunk off *Pen-e-lo-pes* in situ is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk, giving *Pen-Di-* at head. With consistent treatment of the other names – *Cadmi = Ca-*, *Remi = Re-* – the verse order gives
Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*, the word the speaker says the fur will dabis.

Objection acknowledged by majority: on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. Colleagues 1,7,12,18 explicitly concede the Pen- objection is real. Colleague 3 has abandoned the earlier deprecari stem and aligned with Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare.

Unresolved hinge: whether *Pe-* is a principled Latin first syllable of *Penelopes* in situ or an artificial truncation *Pen- → Pe-* licensed only for the first name. Consistency argument: *Cadmi* is not cut to *Ca-d-*, *Remi* not to *Re-mi-*, *Didonis* not to *Di-do-*, so *Penelopes* should not be truncated. Latin scansion defence: *Pe-ne-lo-pes* is normal Latin syllabification and *sequatur* is satisfied without selective truncation.

Current belief: the overwhelming traditional gloss and citation is *pedicare/pedicari*, literal fettering in the pedica/stocks with customary obscene garden pun. The Pen- vs Pe- segmentation objection remains a serious philological challenge; on a literal first-syllable-as-written, consistent treatment the charade builds *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. No definitive metrical/phonological justification for the selective Pen- → Pe- cut has been shown that does not also require analogous cuts for Cadmi/Remi/Didonis.
reflection_text.1:
The method is settled as a syllabic charade built in verse order *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* and *quodque fit ex illis* is the word the *fur deprensus in horto* is told he will *dabis mihi* with which *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Core lexical content is stable: *pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks; *pedicare* = to put in a *pedica*, to fetter the feet, *pedicari* to be fettered/put in stocks. Same form is the classical/medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise/be buggered’, so *in horto* gives the famous dirty garden pun. The punishment inflicted on the thief is the passive/deponent *pedicari/pedicatus*.

Live split remains syllabification of *Penelopes primam* and consistency with *sequatur*.

Pe- camp – Colleagues 1,4,6,7,10-12,15-18 and now Colleague 3 – reads Latin scansion *Pe-ne-lo-pe*, *Penelopes = Pe-ne-lo-pes*. First metrical syllable is *Pe-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* = *Di-* follows it, *primam Cadmi* = *Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi* = *Re-*. *Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = pedicare*. They argue *n* is onset of second syllable *-ne-*, so first metrical syllable is *Pe-*, and *sequatur* is satisfied on a consistent Latin syllabification. That is the received school-room tradition and attested lemma on which the epigram is famously quoted, with literal fettering/stocks sense and customary obscene double sense.

Pen- camp – Colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14 – insists *primam* must be taken of the form as written in the line, *Penelopes = Pen-e-lo-pes*. First spoken chunk in situ is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk, giving *Pen-Di-* at head. *et primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-*. In verse order *Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = pendicare*. They claim *Pe-* reading requires artificial truncation *Pen-* → *Pe-*, amputating *n* that belongs to onset, a cut not applied to *Didonis, Cadmi, Remi*. *sequatur* is evidence for keeping whole first chunk. Colleagues 1,7,12,17,18 now explicitly concede that on strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.

Changes in round 4: Colleague 3 abandoned earlier *deprecari* chain and now aligns with Pe- camp; Colleague 4 now states received tradition is *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* while acknowledging the Pen- literal reading. No new lexical challenge to *pedicare/pedicari* sense.

Unresolved: whether Latin metrical first syllable of *Penelopes* is *Pe-* or phonetic first chunk *Pen-*. If strict first-chunk-as-written is kept consistently with the three other names, verse builds *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*; if traditional Latin scansion *Pe-ne-* is kept, verse builds familiar *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedicari* with fettering/stocks sense and customary obscene garden pun. My current belief remains that the intended, traditionally cited charade is *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare*, literally ‘to be fettered/put in foot-irons/stocks’ and conventionally received as the obscene ‘to be buggered’ garden punishment, while the Pen- vs Pe- syllabification objection is the principal remaining contention and would give *pendicare* on a strictly literal first-chunk reading.
reflection_text.4:
The riddle is a syllabic charade built from the four mythological names in verse order: Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis is the word the fur deprensus in horto is told he will dabis, hac poena culpa luenda tua est.

Method consensus persists: take first syllable piece of each name in the verse order, with Didonis prima sequatur forcing the Dido piece to follow the Penelope piece, and primam Cadmi followed by syllaba prima Remi in the order named.

Dominant tradition = Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare.
* pedica f. = foot-fetter, shackle, stocks; pedicare = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks; pedicari passive/deponent suffered.
Formal school gloss: thief caught in garden threatened with being made pedicatus, to be fettered/shackled/put in foot-irons.
Received jocular gloss: same form is classical/medieval vulgar paedicare/pedicare ‘to sodomise / to be buggered’; epigram traditionally quoted as dirty garden-penalty joke “you will be pedicated / buggered”.

This reading is defended by colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,4,6,7,3. Justification: Latin scansion Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe, so primam of Penelopes in the line is Pe-, not English-style Pen-. Pe- is then followed by Di-, then Ca-, then Re-.

Persistent minority segmentation dispute:
Colleagues 2,9,13,14,5,8 argue literal first spoken chunk of Penelopes as it stands in the line is Pen-, Pen-e-lo-pes. Sequatur then forces Pen- + Di- = Pen-Di-. With primam Cadmi = Ca- and syllaba prima Remi = Re- in order named, this gives Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare, quodque fit ex illis. They claim Pe- requires artificial truncation of natural first syllable Pen- to Pe-, inconsistent with how Didonis, Cadmi, Remi are treated.

Several majority colleagues now explicitly acknowledge the Pen- objection as real philologically. Colleague 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 note the Pe- cut is received school-room tradition that yields familiar attested lemma pedicare/pedicari on which epigram is famous, while conceding strict phonetic first-syllable reading would be Pen-Di-Ca-Re. Colleague 12: “The Pen- objection is real, and on a strictly phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you do get pendicare.” Colleague 1,18 record same concession.

Colleague 13,14 sharpen hinge: primam asked for of form as it stands in verse, Penelopes = Pen-e-lo-pes, first spoken chunk Pen-. Consistency requires same treatment for all four names; no licence to truncate Penelopes only.

Colleague 2,5,8,9 press consistency argument and note concessions, demanding clear metrical/phonological justification for reading Penelopes primam as Pe- rather than natural Pen- in situ, given no analogous truncation for Didonis, Cadmi, Remi.

Unresolved:
* Prosodic segmentation of Penelopes primam: natural Latin first metrical syllable Pe- vs literal first phonetic chunk Pen- as written; sequatur ordering.
* Which meaning is primary: literal fettering/pedicari vs well-known obscene double sense; group largely accepts both coexist, with literal fettering as formal gloss and obscene as traditional jocular reception, primacy remains open.
* Whether pendicare is strictly literal charade product and pedicare is later popularisation.

Remaining marginal proposals earlier: Colleague 3 deprecari chain, Colleague 5 pedicarem variant. In current round Colleague 3 now aligns with pedicare mainstream; Colleague 5 aligns with pendicare consistency argument.

Current best synthesis remains essentially Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare with fettering/shackling penalty, conventionally rendered as obscene pedication joke, while Pen- → pendicare segmentation objection remains consistently pressed by minority and is now explicitly recognized by majority as real philological issue.
reflection_text.7:
The method is now stable across the group: a syllabic charade built in the verse order *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*, *quodque fit ex illis* = the word the *fur deprensus in horto* is told he will *dabis mihi* and with which *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. *Sequatur* is accepted as a real ordering instruction for the first two pieces.

Dispute is now only the cut of *Penelopes primam* and consistency.

Pe- camp – 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,4,6,7:
Latin quantitative scansion: *Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe*, genitive in line *Penelopes = Pe-ne-lo-pes*. *n* is onset of *-ne-*. First metrical syllable taken off the form as it stands is *Pe-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* then puts *Di-* after it → *Pe-Di-*.
*primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in verse order.
Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = *pedicare, quodque fit ex illis*.
*pedica* f. = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter the feet, to put in stocks/foot-irons; *pedicari* to be fettered. That is the formal school-book poena, and the same lemma underlies the classical/medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise’, whence the traditional jocular reception *in horto eris pedicatus*.
This camp now explicitly concedes the Pen- objection: on a strict English phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you get *Pen-* and *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. The defence is that Latin scansion gives *Pe-*, not an English eye-chunk, and that the same principle gives *Ca-* for *Cadmi*, *Re-* for *Remi*, *Di-* for *Didonis*.

Pen- / consistency camp – 2,5,8,9,13,14:
Take the first spoken chunk of the form as it actually stands in the line. *Penelopes* in situ is *Pen-e-lo-pes*; first chunk is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk → *Pen-Di-* head.
Then *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in poet’s order.
Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.
Argument is consistency: why truncate *Penelopes* to *Pe-* while keeping *Didonis = Di-*, *Cadmi = Ca-*, *Remi = Re-* un-truncated? If *primam* means first piece of the form as written and *sequatur* means keep it whole, selective *Pen- → Pe-* is unlicensed. *pendicare* is the literal concatenation; no established lexical poena has been supplied for it, which is the main weakness of this camp.

Colleague 3 remains outlier with *deprecari* chain.

Unresolved hinge: whether *Penelopes primam* is legitimately *Pe-* by Latin scansion *Pe-ne-lo-pes* or must be taken as *Pen-* as written, and whether *sequatur* licenses a selective truncation only for the first name. The Pe- camp has the attested manuscript/school tradition *pedicare/pedicari* with fetter/obscene double sense; the Pen- camp has consistent first-syllable-as-written treatment and the explicit concessions that a phonetic first-chunk reading gives *pendicare*. No principled metrical/phonological justification for the selective *Pe-* cut versus consistent *Ca- / Re- / Di-* treatment has yet been shown to the satisfaction of the Pen- camp.
reflection_text.12:
The charade method is settled in the group: syllabic charade built in the order the verse prescribes, *Didonis prima sequatur* imposes ordering of the second piece after the first, and *quodque fit ex illis* is the word the fur deprensus in horto is told he will *dabis mihi: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- camp
Majority position, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. *Penelopes primam = Pe-*. Latin scansion *Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe*, *Penelopes = Pe-ne-lo-pes*. First metrical syllable of the form as it stands is Pe-; *Didonis prima sequatur = Di-* follows it; *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-*.
Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, *quodque fit ex illis*.
*pedica* f. = foot-fetter, shackle, stocks. *pedicare* lit. ‘to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks/irons’, *pedicari* to be so fettered. Formal school-book poena: the thief is threatened with being made *pedicatus*, fettered/shackled/put in foot-irons/stocks. Same form is classical/medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise, to be buggered’, so the epigram is traditionally quoted as the dirty garden pun *in horto eris pedicatus* – literal fettering, customary reception obscene pedicatio.

Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- camp
Colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14. Strictly phonetic first chunk of the form as written: *Penelopes* in situ is *Pen-e-lo-pes*, first spoken chunk *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* gives *Pen-Di-*. With *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in verse order: *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.
Argument for consistency: we do not truncate *Cadmi* to *Ca-d-* or *Remi* to *Re-mi-* or *Didonis* to *Di-do-*, so we should not truncate *Penelopes* to *Pe-*. The *pedicare* reading requires artificial truncation *Pen- → Pe-* to obtain the familiar attested verb.

Evidence and concessions noted in round 4
* Pe- camp now explicitly states Latin quantitative syllabification *Pe-ne-lo-pes* with n onset of second syllable *-ne-*, hence first metrical syllable Pe-, and *sequatur* satisfied without special pleading. 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 repeat this and note the *Pen-* objection is the English first-phonetic-chunk reading.
* Multiple Pe- colleagues now concede the philological point: 1,12,18,1,7 etc acknowledge that on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. Colleague 12: “The Pen- objection is real, and on a strictly phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you do get pendicare.”
* 13 and 14 sharpen the hinge: *Penelopes primam* is asked for of the form in situ, not abstract lemma; first spoken chunk is *Pen-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* forces *Pen-Di-*. Consistency requires same treatment for *Cadmi*/*Remi*/*Didonis*. They ask for explicit metrical/phonological justification for *Pen- → Pe-* selective cut.
* 2,5,8,9 press the same consistency demand and note the concessions. 2: selective truncation *Penelopes → Pe-* is un-Latin cut licensed for first name only.

Current status
Stable, historically attested solution taught and quoted is *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedicari*, punishment = to be fettered/shackled/put in the stocks, conventionally glossed as obscene pedicatio ‘to be sodomised/buggered’. The *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare* objection remains the main formal challenge, hinging on whether *Penelopes primam* is allowed to be scanned as Latin Pe- or must be taken as the English-looking phonetic chunk Pen-. Colleague 3 moved from deprecari in round 0 to Pe- in round 3 and remains Pe- in round 4. I remain with the Pe- reading as the intended charade and the historically cited lemma, while keeping the Pen- dissent, the explicit concessions about the strict first-chunk reading, and the unresolved question of a principled metrical/phonological justification for the selective Pe- cut versus consistent first-syllable-as-written treatment.
reflection_text.10:
The charade is ordered *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis...* and the verse says the *fur deprensus in horto* will *dabis mihi* that word, *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Core dispute is segmentation of the first name.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,4,6,7: Latin quantitative scansion is decisive.
*Penelope* = Pe-ne-lo-pe, *Penelopes* in the line = Pe-ne-lo-pes. The n is onset of -ne-, so first metrical syllable is Pe-. *Didonis prima sequatur* orders Di- after Pe-, then *primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- in poet’s order. Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re = *pedicare*. 
*Pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks. *Pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter feet/put in stocks; deponent *pedicari* = to be so fettered. Classical-medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* = to sodomise. Hence the classic garden pun: literal fettering, jocularly buggered/pedicatio. This is the school-book gloss and manuscript tradition.

Pen-Di-Ca-Re camp, colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14: literal first-phonetic chunk of the form as written.
The form in the line is *Penelopes*, genitive *Pen-e-lo-pes*. First spoken chunk in situ is Pen-. *sequatur* does real work, so Pen- + Di- = Pen-Di- head. Then *et primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- treated consistently with no truncation of Didonis, Cadmi, Remi. Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = *pendicare*, unattested, the word *quodque fit ex illis* on a strict first-syllable-as-written reading.

Current round shift: Pe- defenders 1,10,11,12,4,7,18 now explicitly concede the philological point: on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of *Penelopes* as written you do get Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare. They maintain Latin scansion licenses Pe- and the received tradition is built on the attested lemma *pedicare/pedicari*.

Unresolved:
1. Segmentation Pe- vs Pen- for *Penelopes primam*. Pe- camp cites Latin syllabification Pe-ne-lo-pes and consistent metrical treatment; Pen- camp cites consistent first-chunk-as-written treatment and the artificiality of amputating n only for the first name.
2. Semantic nuance: literal fettering vs vulgar sodomitical double entendre. Consensus is both co-exist for *pedicare*.

I am still leaning to the dominant consensus *pedicare/pedicari* as the intended word-play with literal fettering in the pedica/stocks and the customary vulgar double sense, because of attestation and the whole manuscript/school-room tradition. The Pen- vs Pe- philological objection is now explicitly conceded by multiple Pe- defenders and the demand for a principled, non-selective justification for reading *Penelopes primam* as Pe- rather than the natural Pen- in situ remains unmet. A consistent literal first-syllable-as-written reading with *sequatur* respected gives *pendicare*, unattested and sense-less, which is why the tradition settles on the Latin-scansion cut Pe-Di-Ca-Re.
reflection_text.18:
The charade method is settled in public discussion: syllabic charade built in the order the verse gives, *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*, *quodque fit ex illis* which the *fur deprensus in horto* is told he will *dabis mihi: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The ordering instruction *Didonis prima sequatur* is doing real work, the concatenation is to be read in poet’s order.

Majority tradition, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,4,6,7:
*Penelopes primam* = Pe-, *Didonis prima sequatur* = Di- follows it, *primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-.
Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = pedicare.
*pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks; *pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks. Suffered form *pedicari*. Literal gloss: garden thief threatened with being fettered/put in foot-irons/stocks.
Vulgar double meaning noted repeatedly: classical/medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* = to sodomise/bugger. The epigram is traditionally quoted as the dirty garden pun “you will be buggered / you will suffer pedication”.
Defence in round 4 is Latin quantitative syllabification: *Penelope* = Pe-ne-lo-pe, *Penelopes* in line = Pe-ne-lo-pes. n is onset of second syllable -ne-. First metrical syllable of form as it stands is Pe-, not English Pen-. Same principle gives Ca- for Cadmi, Re- for Remi, Di- for Didonis. Once Pe- is kept *sequatur* is satisfied without artificial truncation of the other three names and the attested charade word is recovered.

Minority / strict literal, Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is explicit ordering to take first chunk of *Penelopes* as it stands in line and let Dido’s first piece follow it. Form as written is *Penelopes* = Pen-e-lo-pes; first spoken chunk is Pen-, not truncated Pe-. *Sequatur* then gives Pen- + Di- = Pen-Di-.
With *primam Cadmi* = Ca- and *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- in order named, consistent concatenation is Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare, *quodque fit ex illis*.
Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare requires artificial truncation Pen- → Pe- for Penelopes only; the other three names are not similarly truncated. That selective truncation is the point flagged earlier by 2,9 and reasserted in round 4. Colleagues 1,7,12,18 now explicitly concede: on a strict phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you do get Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare. Colleague 12: “The Pen- objection is real, and on a strictly phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written you do get pendicare.”

Errors / disagreements persisting:
Colleague 3 *deprecari* chain D P Re C remains unsupported.
Colleague 5 *Pedicarem* 1st-person future form is morphologically wrong for the charade.

Current understanding:
The intended charade word in the scholarly tradition is pedicare, built on Pe-Di-Ca-Re, with literal sense ‘to fetter/shackle the feet’ and the well-known vulgar pun ‘to be sodomised’, i.e. the thief caught in hortus is threatened with pedication, classically rendered as being fettered/put in stocks and jocularly as being buggered.
Unresolved nuance: the philological objection that *Penelopes primam* is naturally Pen- not Pe- and that a strictly literal first-syllable-as-written reading respecting *sequatur* gives Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare. Majority now explicitly concede the Pen- objection is real and that on strict phonetic first-chunk reading the concatenation is pendicare, while maintaining that the received school-room tradition is Pe- → pedicare with its fetter/vulgar double sense.
No new evidence has changed the core lexical meaning of *pedica/pedicare*; debate remains about segmentation, not semantics once the word is fixed. Need a principled metrical/phonological justification for licensing Pen- → Pe- truncation only for the first name, with no analogous truncation for Didonis, Cadmi, Remi.
reflection_text.16:

The riddle is a syllabic charade with an ordering instruction. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis... fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est.*

Majority position rounds 0-4: Latin quantitative scansion. *Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe, Penelopes = Pe-ne-lo-pes.* The n is onset of -ne-. First metrical syllable that can be taken off the form as it stands in the line is Pe-. *Didonis prima sequatur* puts Di- after Pe-. Then in verse order *primam Cadmi = Ca-* and *syllaba prima Remi = Re-*.

Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re = pedicare, *quodque fit ex illis*.

Formal school gloss: fur deprensus in horto is threatened with pedicari, to be made pedicatus, fettered/shackled/put in foot-irons/stocks. Reception gloss: classical/medieval vulgar paedicare/pedicare = to sodomise/bugger, so the epigram is traditionally quoted as the dirty garden pun *in horto eris pedicatus*: literally fettered, jocularly buggered/pedicatio.

Minority/consistency position rounds 2-4: primam is asked of the form as it stands in the verse. *Penelopes* in situ is Pen-e-lo-pes. Natural first spoken chunk is Pen-. *Didonis prima sequatur* then makes Di- follow the whole first chunk, giving Pen-Di- at the head. With consistent treatment of Cadmi = Ca-, Remi = Re-, the poet’s order yields Pen- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare, *quodque fit ex illis*. The Pe- reading requires an artificial truncation Pen- → Pe- to get the familiar attested lemma pedicare; the truncation is not applied to Didonis, Cadmi, Remi.

The method is now stable and agreed across the group. It is a syllabic charade built in the verse order *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis*. *sequatur* does real ordering work and *quodque fit ex illis* is the word the speaker says the *fur deprensus in horto* will *dabis mihi : hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Two segmentation camps remain.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp – Colleagues 1,4,6,7,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3. 
Argument: Latin quantitative syllabification. *Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe*, *Penelopes* as it stands in the line = *Pe-ne-lo-pes*. The *n* is onset of the second syllable *-ne-*. First metrical syllable is *Pe-*. *Didonis prima sequatur* puts *Di-* after it, then *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-* in verse order. Pe-+Di-+Ca-+Re- = *pedicare*. 
*Pedica* f. = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks. *Pedicare* = to put in a pedica, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks/foot-irons; *pedicari* passive. That is the formal school-book poena: the thief is threatened with being made *pedicatus*, fettered/shackled/put in foot-irons/stocks, *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. 
Same form underlies classical-medieval vulgar *paedicare/pedicare* ‘to sodomise’, whence the traditional jocular garden pun *in horto eris pedicatus*. Majority presents literal fettering as primary with vulgar double sense as customary reception.

Pen-Di-Ca-Re camp – Colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14.
Argument: *primam* is asked of the form as it actually stands in the verse, *Penelopes*, genitive. First spoken chunk off *Pen-e-lo-pes* is *Pen-* . *Didonis prima sequatur* then forces *Di-* to follow that whole chunk → *Pen-Di-*. Then consistent treatment of the other three names in verse order: *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-*, no truncation of *Didonis* to *Di-* with detached *do-*, no analogous cut for *Cadmi/Remi*. Consistency requires the same treatment for *Penelopes*. 
Result: *Pen-* + *Di-* + *Ca-* + *Re-* = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*, *quodque fit ex illis* which the fur is said to dare.

Middle acknowledgement now explicit. Colleagues 1,7,12,17,18 concede the philological objection is real on a strict English phonetic first-chunk reading of the genitive as written: you do get *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*. They maintain the Latin scansion defence for *Pe-*.

Unresolved carried forward:
- Philological/metrical licence for *Penelopes primam = Pe-* vs natural first spoken chunk *Pen-* in situ, and why a selective *Pen- → Pe-* truncation is allowed only for the first name while *Didonis, Cadmi, Remi* keep their natural first pieces.
- Whether the penalty should be reported as the attested *pedicare/pedicari* with literal fetter/stocks sense and customary obscene double entendre, or as *pendicare* on strict first-syllable-as-written consistency, which would require re-evaluation of lemma and meaning; *pendicare* is unattested/senseless.
- Final wording of the poena: literal fettering/shackling/stocks, the vulgar sodomy sense, or both as double entendre. Majority still favours *pedicare* with fettering primary and obscene as customary reception.

Earlier minority deviations dropped: Colleague 3 abandoned *deprecari* chain and now follows Pe-Di-Ca-Re with literal fetter and vulgar double sense.
